title: AWS IAM Revision Notes: Identities, Policies, MFA and Keys
summary: Quick revision of AWS IAM: users, groups, roles, policies and least privilege, how policy evaluation and explicit deny work, and securing access with MFA, the root account and roles instead of access keys.

chapters.title: AWS IAM at a Glance
points: Users, groups and roles
Policies and least privilege
Policy evaluation and explicit deny
MFA and the root account
Access keys vs roles

chapters.title: Users, Groups and Roles Mental Model
points: Definition: IAM is the global AWS service that decides who (authentication) can do what on which resource (authorization); principals are users, roles and the root account
Mechanism: a user is a long-lived identity with a password and/or access keys; a group is only a container of users for attaching policies and cannot contain groups or be a principal
Comparison: user = permanent credentials for one person or app; role = no credentials of its own, assumed through STS to get temporary credentials (default 1 hour, max 12 hours)
Example: an EC2 instance profile wraps a role so the app on the instance gets rotating credentials with no keys stored on disk
Interview Point: Can a group be a principal in a policy? What is the difference between a user and a role? How does a role get credentials? Who can assume a role (trust policy)?

chapters.title: Policies, Least Privilege and Evaluation Logic
points: Definition: a policy is a JSON document of statements with Effect, Action, Resource and optional Condition; least privilege means granting only the actions and resources a task needs
Mechanism: evaluation starts at implicit deny, then any explicit Deny wins, otherwise an Allow is needed; an explicit Deny always overrides every Allow

Comparison: identity-based policies attach to users, groups or roles; resource-based policies attach to a resource (S3 bucket, role trust policy) and name a Principal; permission boundaries and SCPs only limit the maximum and never grant
Example: Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket/* plus a Deny with a condition aws:SourceIp or aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent=false blocks access even if another policy allows it

Interview Point: What is the default for a request with no matching policy? Does an Allow ever override an explicit Deny? How do SCPs and permission boundaries differ from identity policies? How would you find the permissions a role really uses (Access Analyzer, last accessed data)?

chapters.title: MFA, Root Account and Access Keys vs Roles
points: Definition: MFA adds a second factor (virtual TOTP app, FIDO2 security key or hardware token) on top of the password; the root account is the all-powerful email-based identity created with the account

Mechanism: lock down root with MFA, no access keys and use only for the few root-only tasks (change the root email or password, close the account, restore a locked-out IAM admin); do daily work as an IAM user or via IAM Identity Center

Comparison: access keys are long-lived (AKIA...) and leak through code and git; role credentials are temporary (ASIA... plus session token) and expire automatically, so prefer roles for EC2, Lambda and CI
Example: enforce MFA by denying all actions except MFA setup when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false, and rotate or delete any access key unused for 90 days
Interview Point: Why should the root account have no access keys? When do you still need an access key? How do you enforce MFA with a policy? How do applications on EC2 get credentials without keys?

chapters.title: Everyday IAM Commands and Common Mistakes
points: Definition: day-to-day IAM work is create identity, attach policy, test, then review; aws sts get-caller-identity shows which principal your CLI is actually using

Mechanism: aws iam create-user, create-group, add-user-to-group, attach-group-policy --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess; aws iam simulate-principal-policy tests whether an action is allowed before you ship it
Comparison: AWS managed policies are maintained by AWS and broad; customer managed policies are reusable and tailored; inline policies are embedded in one identity and die with it

Mistakes: attaching AdministratorAccess or Action * on Resource * to fix an AccessDenied, attaching policies to users instead of groups, committing keys to git, and forgetting that a trust policy as well as a permissions policy is needed to assume a role

Interview Point: How do you debug an AccessDenied error? Managed vs inline policy: when would you pick each? How do you check who you are in the CLI? What goes wrong when a role is assumable by Principal *?

chapters.title: AWS IAM Cheat Sheet
points: Evaluation order: implicit deny, then explicit Deny wins, then Allow; Deny always beats Allow
Groups hold users only; policies attach to groups; roles are assumed and give temporary credentials
Root: enable MFA, delete keys, use only for root-only tasks; everyone else uses roles or Identity Center
Commands: aws sts get-caller-identity, aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name X, aws iam simulate-principal-policy
Key prefixes: AKIA = long-lived user key, ASIA = temporary role key; prefer roles, rotate or delete unused keys
